catalog_citation: Mugele, Robert & Michael Rodewald. 1991. Aspects of Bandi tonology. Studies in African Linguistics 22(2): 105-134. doi:10.32473/sal.v22i2.107425
catalog_locator: p. 105 (PDF p. 1 of 30): abstract, and section 1 Introduction, first two sentences; supporting p. 106 sec. 2.1 (PDF p. 2) and p. 121 sec. 3.2.3 (PDF p. 17)
catalog_quote: Bandi tonology offers three points of interest. The first is low tone opacity. Several tone rules act to obscure the presence of underlying low tones in Bandi. In some cases low tones are lost completely while in other cases underlying low tones are manifested phonetically as downstep tones or as the low of a falling glide. The net result of Bandi tone rules is to create considerable opacity with respect to low tones. Second, is the treatment of polarizing tones. In Bandi, polarization rules cannot merely create a new tone, but must assign tone height to an underlying tone of unspecified tone height. [...] 1. Introduction. The Bandi language has a rich tonal system that provides numerous challenges for the analyst. Few studies of Bandi tonology exist, and they are limited in scope. [...] H Tone Spread (HTS) operates throughout the speech string. Consequently phrase final L's are heard as falling tones. [...] However, there is no evidence for a synchronic mid tone in Bandi. We merely speculate here that polarizing tones such as those in Bandi may have a historical source as mid tones in a three level tone system that later collapsed into a two level system.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: No source opened states where word stress falls in Bandi. The only first-hand primary description obtained (Mugele & Rodewald 1991, condensing Rodewald 1989) treats Bandi purely as a two-tone (H/L) lexical-tone language with phrase-level tone rules (H tone spread, contour simplification, downstep, polarizing tones, LLH melodies) and never mentions stress, accent or prominence. Hintze 1948 (based on Heydorn 1940-41) likewise only notes, fn. 1 p. 164, 'Alle hier behandelten Sprachen sind Tonsprachen' (all languages treated here, Bandi included, are tone languages). Family-level second-hand statements: Vydrin 2017 p. 34 'Stress is absent in the majority of Mande languages; where identifiable (e.g. Bamana) its functional load is small'; Dwyer 1981 (Lorma handbook, Mande appendix) 'While stress is generally non-contrastive in Mande it is generally distinctive. In Kpelle it falls on the first high-toned syllable..' -- neither is about Bandi specifically.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Mugele & Rodewald note all tone rules operate in the domain of the phrase (phonetic rules) or in limited morphemic environments (morphological rules).
new_statements.domain_note: Mugele & Rodewald 1991 analyse tone at word and phrase level (isolation forms vs. phrase-medial forms; 'H Tone Spread operates throughout the speech string'). Nothing said about stress at word or phrase level. Vydrin 2017 remark is family-level; Dwyer 1981 remark is generic Mande with a Kpelle rule.
new_statements.identity_note: All Bandi-specific sources examined describe Liberian Bandi of Lofa County (Kolahun district). Mugele & Rodewald 1991 (data from Rodewald's 6.5 years with the Institute for Liberian Languages) covers the six Bandi clans, 96.5% cognate; Hintze 1948 relies solely on Heydorn 1940-41 (north-western Liberia; Yawiazu named as a dialect). No differently named variety involved; glottocode band1352.

sources.note: Generic Mande statement, not Bandi-specific: 'While stress is generally non-contrastive in Mande it is generally distinctive. In Kpelle, it falls on the first high-toned syllable in the word, or if the word has no high tones, it falls on the first syllable. Stress is acoustically marked by an increase in the loudness of the syllable..' Bandi named only as a SW Mande language sharing initial consonant change.
